global.headline: COLOMBIA EARTHQUAKE RESCUE ENTERS "FINAL PHASE" AS TOLL PASSES 265, GOVERNMENT LIMITS FOREIGN AID TO FOUR COUNTRIES
summary: Colombia's rescue effort after Monday's 7.4-magnitude earthquake entered what officials called its "final phase" on Wednesday as the critical 72-hour survival window closed. Confirmed deaths stand at 265, with more than 3,500 injured and almost 500 still missing. In Pereira, crews spent a third night working with cranes, sniffer dogs and vibration-detection equipment around a collapsed bakery, focused on street vendor Pablo Loaiza after picking up possible signs of life; relatives gathered nearby as rescuers called for silence around the rubble.

The government has also stirred controversy by saying it will request rescue teams from only four countries — the US, El Salvador, Ecuador and Israel — citing certification requirements, after Mexico said its renowned "Topos" rescue brigade had its offer turned down. Foreign Minister Omar Bula denied any country had been excluded on ideological grounds, but the episode has exposed administrative confusion in a five-week-old government handling its first major disaster.
global.geopolitical: A newly installed administration's decision to narrow the field of foreign rescue teams accepted, and its public spat with Mexico over a rejected offer, is becoming its own test of President De La Espriella's diplomatic and crisis-management credibility barely a month into office, on top of the earlier volatility in its own casualty counting.
global.socioeconomic: As the search for survivors gives way to recovery, attention is shifting to the far costlier task of rebuilding Chocó and Valle del Cauca's housing stock and infrastructure, with the government's handling of both foreign aid and reconstruction financing likely to shape how the disaster is remembered politically.

global.headline: POLAND FOILS RUSSIAN PLOT TO KILL A US CITIZEN ON NATO SOIL; BOMB KILLS A DEFECTOR IN CRIMEA
summary: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Poland's security service and police detained a Russian man on 7 August who had been recruited by Moscow to assassinate a dual Ukrainian-American citizen in Warsaw, someone Tusk said was "inconvenient to the Putin regime." Tusk called it the first known instance of an attack ordered by Russia against a US citizen inside another NATO country's territory, and noted it follows the June killing of a Russian dissident artist in the Polish town of Biała Podlaska.

Separately in occupied Crimea, a bomb hidden in a rubbish bin killed a Russian naval officer in Sevastopol on Thursday. Unofficial Telegram channels identified him as Robert Shageev, the former commander of Ukraine's only submarine, the Zaporizhzhia, who defected to Russia when it annexed Crimea in 2014 and went on to command a Russian Black Sea Fleet submarine. Sevastopol's governor blamed Ukrainian intelligence; a woman has been arrested on suspicion of planting the device.
global.geopolitical: A Kremlin-ordered assassination attempt against a US citizen inside NATO territory is a direct test of the alliance's tolerance for Russian covert action on its own soil, even as Kyiv's intelligence services appear to be running parallel lethal operations against Russian-aligned targets inside occupied Crimea — a shadow war now running in both directions across the conflict's edges.
global.socioeconomic: Each confirmed plot adds to the security and surveillance burden NATO states already carry for Ukrainian refugees, dual nationals and defectors on their soil, a cost that compounds the longer the war's covert dimension keeps expanding beyond the battlefield itself.

global.headline: UKRAINE STRIKES RUSSIA'S NOVOROSSIYSK GRAIN TERMINALS AND NAVAL BASE, HALTING WORK AT ONE OF THE WORLD'S BUSIEST WHEAT PORTS
summary: Ukraine launched a large overnight drone and missile attack on Russia's Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, damaging three major grain terminals and halting their operations. A loading gallery at United Grain Co.'s Novorossiysk Grain Plant collapsed and several silos were damaged; a loading gallery and truck-unloading facility at rival operator Demetra's terminal were also hit. President Volodymyr Zelensky said the strikes also targeted Russian naval vessels in the bay, including the frigates Admiral Essen and Admiral Makarov, a large landing ship and a corvette. Regional governor Veniamin Kondratyev said three people were killed, including an eight-year-old child, and 24 injured.

Russia is the world's largest wheat exporter and ships most of that grain through Novorossiysk, making the terminal damage a direct hit on global food-supply infrastructure rather than purely a military target.
global.geopolitical: Striking Russia's principal grain-export gateway alongside its Black Sea Fleet assets marks a deliberate widening of Ukraine's campaign from military and energy targets to the infrastructure underpinning Russia's export economy, raising the odds of a harder Russian response and further complicating any renewed Black Sea grain-corridor diplomacy.
global.socioeconomic: Damage serious enough to halt loading at some of Russia's largest grain terminals threatens to tighten global wheat supply and lift prices just as several import-dependent economies are already contending with elevated food costs from other war-driven disruptions this year.

global.headline: ISRAELI TROOPS DISMANTLE SETTLER OUTPOSTS IN WEST BANK SIEGE, BUT AN EVICTION ORDER FOR THE BESIEGED FAMILY SPARKS OUTCRY
summary: Israeli forces returned to the West Bank village of Qusra near Nablus for a second time overnight Wednesday into Thursday, dismantling two settler outposts and detaining one Israeli, as a four-day siege of Palestinian homes — including one belonging to a US citizen — continued. Israel's military briefly ordered around 20 Palestinians to evacuate 15 homes in the area, a move it said was meant to help clear the harassing settlers, but reversed the order after it drew public attention; some residents were able to return, though one of the two besieged families told reporters they still could not reach their house. The village's mayor said the army told him the operation would continue until Sunday morning.

US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, a longtime, vocal supporter of the settler movement, broke sharply with that record on Thursday, calling the siege "an act of terror" and the settlers' conduct "disgusting" and "thuggish," and saying Israel had acted at Washington's request.
global.geopolitical: A pro-settler US ambassador publicly branding a settler siege "terror," paired with the Israeli military's own botched attempt to evict the victims rather than their besiegers, exposes real strain inside a relationship that has usually treated settler violence as a domestic Israeli matter rather than one requiring blunt American intervention.
global.socioeconomic: Days of cut water and electricity aimed at a handful of families is a small-scale but illustrative version of the broader displacement pattern the UN has already flagged this year — more than 1,430 settler-violence incidents and roughly 3,800 Palestinians displaced — where sustained economic pressure, not formal eviction, does the work of pushing residents out.

global.headline: MASSIVE OIL SPILL FROM A GROUNDED "SHADOW FLEET" TANKER REACHES OMAN'S COASTLINE
summary: A slick from the tanker Caroline Bezengi, grounded and partly submerged off Oman since suffering unexplained explosions near Yemen in early June, has spread largely unchecked for weeks and reached Oman's coastline this week, contaminating beaches around Ras Madrakah roughly 200km north of Qabiliyah Island. The spill now covers more than 2,000 square kilometres, and experts warn it threatens to become one of the world's worst in years.

The 247-metre vessel, which had loaded nearly a million barrels of oil, is believed to be part of Russia's sanctions-evading "shadow fleet" and is under both UK and EU sanctions for carrying Russian crude. No party has claimed responsibility for the June explosions, and there has been no official explanation of what caused them.
global.geopolitical: A sanctioned shadow-fleet tanker left to leak unchecked for weeks off Oman is a reminder that the ageing, poorly insured, badly regulated vessels sanctions regimes have pushed into the shadows carry environmental risks that fall on whichever coastline they happen to founder near, regardless of who is actually enforcing the sanctions.
global.socioeconomic: A spill of this scale threatens Oman's fisheries and coastal tourism industries with cleanup and compensation costs that will likely fall largely on Omani authorities and insurers rather than the tanker's opaque ownership structure, in a Gulf shipping corridor already strained by the Iran war's separate disruptions.

singapore.headline: WORKERS' PARTY CHIEF PRITAM SINGH STRUCK OFF LAW SOCIETY ROLLS OVER PERJURY CONVICTION
summary: Singapore's Court of Three Judges — Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon, Justice Kannan Ramesh and Justice See Kee Oon — unanimously ordered Workers' Party chief and Leader of the Opposition Pritam Singh struck off the rolls of advocates and solicitors on Thursday, following a 20-minute hearing, and ordered him to pay S$5,808 in costs. The Law Society's counsel, Senior Counsel Cavinder Bull, argued there were "no exceptional circumstances that mitigate a strike-off," and that Singh's roles as MP and Opposition Leader "aggravate the negative impact" of his conduct rather than excuse it. Singh declined to comment as he left the courtroom.

The disciplinary action followed Singh's February 2025 conviction on two counts of lying under oath to the Committee of Privileges in the Raeesah Khan affair, and his unsuccessful December 2025 appeal, after which he paid a S$14,000 fine. Singh is a non-practising lawyer, so the strike-off affects his formal professional standing rather than an active legal practice; his parliamentary seat and party leadership are unaffected by the ruling.
singapore.socioeconomic: The ruling closes out the legal consequences of the Raeesah Khan saga for Singh personally, but leaves the Workers' Party to manage the symbolism of its leader being the first sitting Leader of the Opposition struck off as a lawyer, even as his political mandate as an elected MP remains untouched.

singapore.headline: OVER 2.4 MILLION SINGAPOREANS TO GET UP TO $600 COST-OF-LIVING PAYMENT FROM SEPT 9
summary: The Ministry of Finance announced that more than 2.4 million Singapore citizens aged 21 and above will receive between S$400 and S$600 under the Enhanced Budget 2026 Cost-of-Living Special Payment, disbursed automatically from 9 September. Eligibility is based on owning no more than one property and an Assessable Income for Year of Assessment 2025 of up to S$100,000, with the Annual Value of a recipient's home factored in so lower-income households get more support.
Citizens are encouraged to link their NRIC to PayNow by 30 August to receive the payment on the earliest possible date; eligibility can be checked via Singpass on the govbenefits.gov.sg portal.
singapore.geopolitical: Fits a now-familiar pattern of successive Singapore cost-of-living transfers this year, part of the government's broader response to a global inflationary backdrop shaped in part by the Iran war's effect on energy and shipping costs.
singapore.socioeconomic: A further targeted cash transfer on top of this year's earlier GST Voucher and Middle-East-war support packages underscores how central direct fiscal relief has become to the government's cost-of-living strategy, even as core inflation stays elevated into next year per MAS's own guidance.

singapore.headline: SINGAPOREAN FUGITIVE KIDNAPPED IN JOHOR BAHRU, RESCUED WITH GIRLFRIEND AFTER RANSOM NEGOTIATION
summary: A 32-year-old Singaporean man wanted by Singapore police, who had been hiding illegally in Malaysia since May, was kidnapped by six people who demanded S$80,000 for his release — later negotiated down to S$25,000. His captors slashed both his thighs and sent his mother a photo of him blindfolded and bound to prove they meant business; she lodged a police report and transferred S$5,000 before the planned ransom drop.

Royal Malaysia Police arrested a 40-year-old suspect at a supermarket in Nusa Bestari, Iskandar Puteri, rescuing the man and his 33-year-old girlfriend, who was also held. Five of the six suspects, all Malaysians with prior criminal records, tested positive for methamphetamine at the time of arrest.
singapore.geopolitical: The latest in a string of kidnap-for-ransom cases against Singaporeans in Johor this year, again resolved through swift Malaysian-Singaporean police cooperation, though this one underscores a starker vulnerability: fugitives sheltering across the border have no route to official protection and become easy targets themselves.
singapore.socioeconomic: The case is a reminder that criminal syndicates operating along the Johor-Singapore border increasingly treat vulnerable individuals — including Singaporeans hiding from their own authorities — as a ready source of ransom income.

word.definition: Harsh public condemnation or verbal abuse; the state of disgrace or discredit that results from being widely criticised.
word.etymology: From Late Latin obloquium ("contradiction, speaking against"), from Latin ob- ("against") + loqui ("to speak"); entered English in the 15th century through ecclesiastical and legal Latin.
word.example: Singapore's opposition leader faced a courtroom's formal obloquy on Thursday, struck from the rolls for lying under oath, the same day the US ambassador to Israel heaped a very different kind on West Bank settlers, branding their siege of a Palestinian family "an act of terror."
